meta.description: Goldwyn denied it. The phrase is in print from 1934 with no name on it, and this exact wording only from 1946.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Gentlemen, You May Include Me Out'?
meta.ogDescription: The most famous Goldwynism — which Goldwyn denied, and which appears in print before anyone attached his name to it.

answer.label: Not documented as Goldwyn’s — and this wording is from 1946
answer.authorDates: The phrase is in print from February 1934 with no name attached
answer.sourceLine: Samuel Goldwyn denied saying it. Profiled in LIFE in February 1959 he insisted he had said “Gentlemen, I’m withdrawing from the association” and that “by the time I got back to the studio, it was all over town I’d said, ‘Include me out.’” Quote Investigator ↗’s earliest located instance has no Goldwyn in it at all: a February 1934 newspaper serialization of the 1933 film Let’s Fall In Love, in which a producer character says “Include me out of it.” Alva Johnston pinned the line to Goldwyn in 1937 as “Gentlemen, include me out”; the longer wording asked about here first shows up in Louis Untermeyer’s A Treasury of Laughter in 1946.

source.heading: Where this exact wording comes from

source.excerpt: It took place at a long conference of directors, producers, and bigwigs. They were all trying to induce Goldwyn to join them in a project which he disliked. Finally he turned to them and said, “Gentlemen, the best I can give you is a definite maybe.” Then, a few minutes later, he said, “I’ve reconsidered my decision. Gentlemen, you may include me out.”
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ gives the earliest instance as a newspaper serialization of the 1933 Columbia film Let’s Fall In Love, published 19 February 1934 in the Tyrone Daily Herald, page 5, column 2. The speaker is Max, a film producer in the story, and the line is “Include me out of it.” QI notes Herbert Fields wrote the story and screenplay but that it is not clear who wrote the serialization.

Through the mid-1930s the phrase keeps appearing with nobody’s name on it: an unidentified man at a Chicago business meeting in June Provines’s Chicago Tribune column of 27 March 1935, a “prominent film executive” in Sheilah Graham’s column in 1936, “our pet producer” in 1937 — all dated and cited by QI ↗.

Goldwyn enters in 1937, with Alva Johnston’s The Great Goldwyn — serialized in the Saturday Evening Post that May, per QI ↗. We read the book itself, which the Internet Archive serves in full view ↗: at page 16 Johnston writes that an ordinary man quitting the Hays organization might have said “Gentlemen, I prefer to stand aloof”, and that “Sam said, ‘Gentlemen, include me out.’” Note the form — Johnston has no “you may” in it. The longer wording on this page QI dates to Untermeyer’s A Treasury of Laughter, page 253, which the Internet Archive’s catalogue record ↗ dates to 1946.

Goldwyn denied it on the record. QI quotes ↗ the LIFE profile of 16 February 1959: “None of them are true. They’re all made up by a bunch of comedians and pinned on me … It’s ridiculous. It’s a lie.” QI ends with two scenarios — Goldwyn said something like it in 1933 or earlier and it spread, or a Hollywood quipster made it up and publicists hung it on him — and does not choose between them. Neither do we.

Johnston knew the problem even as he wrote. On the same page, read in that full-view scan ↗, he warns that “today it takes an expert to pick the genuine Goldwyn lines from the spurious. More people are counterfeiting on Goldwyn than on Uncle Sam” — and then files “include me out” among what he calls the true ones. That is a judgement by the man who put the line into general circulation, not independent evidence for it.

author.heading: About Samuel Goldwyn
author.metaLine: 1882–1974 · Polish-born American film producer and studio founder
author.bio: Samuel Goldwyn (1882–1974) was a Polish-born American film producer and a pioneer of the American film industry, who produced what is described as the United States’s first major motion picture and was a founding contributor and executive of several studios. He received the Irving G. Thalberg Memorial Award (1947), the Jean Hersholt Humanitarian Award (1958) and the Cecil B. DeMille Award (1973). He is named here because the line is told about him — not because the record shows he said it.

misattribution.heading: The most famous Goldwynism, and the one he denied
misattribution.intro: This is the line Goldwyn is best known for and the line he most flatly disowned. The record does not settle it either way, so neither does this page.

items.tag: Denied by him; unresolved by QI
items.why: Goldwyn told LIFE in 1959 that he had said “Gentlemen, I’m withdrawing from the association” and that the Goldwynisms were “all made up by a bunch of comedians and pinned on me”. Quote Investigator ↗ finds no citation naming him before Alva Johnston’s 1937 biography, three years after the phrase was already in print — but allows a scenario in which he did say it in 1933 or earlier and the phrase escaped into Hollywood from there. Wikiquote ↗ files it under Misattributed, citing Boller and George, They Never Said It (1990), p. 40.

Johnston’s 1937 version, the one that made the line famous, is the short form — we read it at page 16 of the full-view scan ↗: “Sam said, ‘Gentlemen, include me out.’” “Gentlemen, you may include me out” is longer and later: QI ↗ dates it to Untermeyer’s anthology in the 1940s, and Bennett Cerf’s Try and Stop Me (1944) gives a third form, “Gentlemen, kindly include me out.”

items.who: An unnamed Chicago businessman, and “our pet producer”
items.why: Before any name stuck, QI documents ↗ the phrase in a 1935 Chicago Tribune column about a meeting at the Hotel Sherman and in Sheilah Graham’s Hollywood columns of 1936 and 1937, each time with the speaker left anonymous. A line that floats like that usually has no single author to find.

misattribution.truthLine: Best evidence: the phrase is documented from 19 February 1934, in a newspaper serialization of Let’s Fall In Love, with no Goldwyn in it; this exact wording from Louis Untermeyer’s A Treasury of Laughter (1946), p. 253 — both per Quote Investigator ↗, which leaves the authorship open.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Samuel Goldwyn (1882–1974) was a Polish-born producer and studio founder, and by the 1930s he was famous enough that a whole genre of jokes — “Goldwynisms” — could be manufactured in his voice. Being the man the gags got pinned on is its own kind of fame, and he knew it.
The LIFE denial is the best part of the story. He protested that the lines were invented and hung on him, then, as QI quotes the reporter ↗, “hid something, perhaps a smile, behind his napkin.”
detailsBody: The chronology QI assembles is the useful thing here: a 1934 film serialization, an anonymous 1935 businessman, two anonymous Hollywood columns, then a biography in 1937 that gives the line a speaker, then anthologies in 1944 and 1946 that smooth the wording, then a studio history in 1969 and a memoir in 1975 retelling it as settled fact. The confidence grows at every step while the evidence does not.

David Niven put the sceptical case in Bring On the Empty Horses (1975), listing the famous Goldwynisms and asking — in a passage QI quotes ↗ — “who can claim to have been present when these pearls of wisdom were dropped?”
context.pull: He denied it to LIFE in 1959 with a straight face — and, the reporter noticed, a napkin.

Read directly at p. 16 of the 1937 Random House printing: "An ordinary man, on deciding to quit the Hays organization, might have turned to his fellow producers and said, ‘Gentlemen, I prefer to stand aloof’ ... Sam said, ‘Gentlemen, include me out.’" The same page reads "today it takes an expert to pick the genuine Goldwyn lines from the spurious. More people are counterfeiting on Goldwyn than on Uncle Sam." No "you may" form appears in the book.
